slides.say: A B C D is a rectangle. E lies on A D, G lies on B C, and F lies on A B. A E is three times E D, and B G is three times G C. Triangles F E G and E G C are shaded. Which of the following additional data is sufficient to determine the total shaded area?
at: A B C D is a rectangle

slides.say: The wording isn't very clear. What do they want? They ask which one piece of data, if they gave it to us, would be enough to calculate the shaded area. [short pause] We'll use the symmetry principle from the last lesson.

[short pause] First, the figure. E cuts A D into two pieces, three to one, and G cuts B C the same way, three to one. So E is exactly above G, and E G is a straight line from top to bottom. It cuts the rectangle into a left rectangle and a right rectangle. And F? Nobody told us where F is on A B. Remember that.
Let's start with the data that works, the area of E C D. They don't say how big it is, so let's call it s. It could be ten, or a hundred, any number.
E C is a diagonal of the right rectangle, so it cuts it into two equal halves. That means the shaded triangle E G C is also s, and the right rectangle is s plus s, two s.
at: the shaded triangle E G C

slides.say: The left rectangle has the same height, and its base is three times longer, three to one. So it's three times as big, three times two s, which is six s.

And the shaded triangle F E G? Its base is E G, the whole side of the left rectangle, and its tip F is on the opposite side, A B. That's the symmetry principle again, so it's half of the left rectangle, three s. Together, the shaded area is s plus three s, four s. So if they give us the area of E C D, we can find the shaded area.
at: And the shaded triangle F E G

slides.say: Some students see it even faster. The whole rectangle is eight s, the shaded part is half of it, and E C D is an eighth. In the exam, once we've understood this, we mark choice number one and move on.
[pause] We're in a lesson, so let's see why the other choices fail. Choice number two, the area of A F E. Say it's s. A F E is half of a small rectangle at the top, so that rectangle is two s.
at: Choice number two, the area of A F E
A F E is half of a small

slides.say: But how big is the rectangle under it? We can't know, because we don't know where F is. If they told us that F is the middle of A B, the two parts would match. They didn't. So even with a number, five, ten or twenty, we can't find the shaded area. Choice number two is out.
at: how big is the rectangle under it

slides.say: Choice number three, the area of F B G, has exactly the same problem. We don't know where F is. It's out too.

And choice number four says none of the data is enough, but we already saw that the area of E C D is enough. So it's out, and choice number one is our answer. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
at: choice number one is our answer
